<context query="WebSocket subprotocol access token logging" template="default" budget="8000">
<section name="Conventions" source="repo" priority="1">
<document source="specs/support-agent-hal-subprotocol-offer/spec.md" type="spec" relevance="1.00" tokens="491">
## The api part

- **FR-001**: `apps/api`'s WebSocket authentication MUST read the offered token as the first `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value that is not `hal.v1`, through HAL Engine's `credentialFromSubprotocol`, in either order; from HAL Engine 0.5.0 a bare token offered without the marker yields no token (#203), and an `Authorization` header is read only when it names the offered token or no token is offered; from HAL Engine 0.7.0 the engine itself refuses a header and an offered token that differ with `400` before this runs (FR-037 in support-agent-tms-access).
- **FR-002**: An offer of `hal.v1` alone carries no token and MUST be refused by the existing WebSocket auth check, as `044` requires of a connection without a token.
- **FR-003**: A real access token from the api's own token route, three dot-joined base64url segments, offered as `['hal.v1', <token>]` MUST pass the client's subprotocol character check, complete the handshake against the api's own composition, and leave the socket's `protocol` equal to `'hal.v1'`.
- **FR-004**: The handshake response MUST answer `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: hal.v1` and carry the token in no response header.
- **FR-005**: While HAL Engine accepted the deprecated shape, a bare-token offer still connected, so a browser on the previous bundle was not cut off during the rollout. From HAL Engine 0.5.0, which dropped that shape, a bare-token offer MUST be refused, which every shipped client already avoids by offering `hal.v1` (#203).
- **FR-006**: The engine's exported `HAL_WS_SUBPROTOCOL` MUST equal `'hal.v1'`.
- **FR-007**: Lapsed with #181, which removed the frame recorder of [support-agent-chat](../support-agent-chat/spec.md). While it existed, the recorder offered `[HAL_WS_SUBPROTOCOL, token]` and re-running it against the pinned engine reproduced the committed fixture with an empty diff, since the handshake produces no frame of its own; FR-003 and FR-011 carry the offer on each side. (#181)
</document>
<document source="specs/support-agent-chat/spec.md" type="spec" relevance="0.51" tokens="805">
## Sources

- `hal-engine/docs/websocket-protocol.md` §2.2 (token as subprotocol), §4.1, §5.2-5.8 (frame semantics, the normative source for the reducer requirements), and `:294-296` (the terminal-frame clause #14 read and #148 inverts).
- HAL Engine `src/transport/ws/sender.ts` and `messageHandler.ts` (suppression, frame order, error path; `messageHandler.ts:72-80` forwards the tool-authored `clientMessages` index without renumbering, which `multiRoundSuppressed` records), `connectionHandler.ts` (subprotocol to `Bearer`, session deleted on close), `src/transport/createServer.ts:41-44` (marker selection) and `src/index.ts:19-28` (the eager barrel export that forbids a browser import).
- `ws@8.20.0` `lib/websocket.js:962-963` (refusal of an unanswered offer) and `:770-776` (the subprotocol charset the token is validated against).
- ADR-004 in `the-expert-ui` (one socket per session, `WebSocketCtor` test seam, one-shot reconnect), copied in shape but not in rationale.
- `the-expert/src/api/chat-router.ts:89-96`: the org's precedent of surfacing "the chat has expired" rather than "the chat does not exist", cited via HAL Engine's `hal-engine-session-expiry-lookup` (#141).
- HAL Engine `ErrorCodes` (`RATE_LIMITED`, `INVALID_MESSAGE`, `SERVER_ERROR`, `INVALID_FORMAT`, and from 0.7.0 `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE`, `TIMEOUT` and `UPSTREAM_ERROR`) and HAL Engine's `hal-engine-provider-failover` (#91), which established that connection-class messages persist.
- CFOAgent's `gemini.ts` `statusMessages` map, streamed as a `status` event: the same problem solved server-side, and the `` `Executing ${toolName}...` `` counter-example it ships in production. HAL Engine's wire protocol gives `ToolEntry` only `toolName` and `toolInput`, and the tool contract's rule that nothing may push entries the client does not render blocks routing a server-authored sentence through `clientMessages`, so the sentence is chosen client-side.
- bowman-ui: `bowman-ui-toast` (#75, the `duration={null}` mechanism), `bowman-ui-message-list` (#78) and `bowman-ui-chat-composer` (#77) (the pinning expression and composer growth), `bowman-ui-composer-resize-browser` (#132) and `bowman-ui-consumer-app` (#82) (why this is the first repo with a real browser, and the `375x667` viewport precedent). No org precedent for browser testing exists beyond `bowman-ui-consumer-app`'s config.
- The issue sequences quoted in FR-017, FR-018, FR-031 and FR-032 (the commit-before-error ordering and the mid-stream probe) are the normative examples for the run lifecycle and `interrupted` requirements.
- Merged per-ticket specs: `support-agent-chat-wiring` (#14), `support-agent-persistent-connection-notices` (#40), `support-agent-danish-failure-messages` (#48), `support-agent-tool-activity-adoption` (#146), `support-agent-chat-screen-browser-check` (#156), `support-agent-adopt-recorded-frames` (#181), `support-agent-expired-conversation-notice` (#187), `support-agent-busy-terminal-contract` (#191), `support-agent-hal-subprotocol-offer` (#192), `support-agent-reconnect-session-id` (#203), `support-agent-interrupted-answer-detection` (#206), from OLT issues `044`, `098`, `117`, `137`, `147`, `172`, `178`, `182`, `183`, `194` and `197`.
</document>
</section>
<section name="Relevant Code" source="code" priority="2">
<document source="apps/api/src/oauth/bearerToken.ts" type="code" relevance="1.00" tokens="209">
export interface BearerHeaders {
  authorization?: string;
  // eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/naming-convention -- a browser WebSocket can only carry its token as the offered subprotocol.
  'sec-websocket-protocol'?: string;
}

// RFC 6750 Authorization header, or the token a browser WebSocket offers beside the hal.v1 marker since it cannot set headers.
export function bearerTokenOf(headers: BearerHeaders): string | undefined {
  const offered = credentialFromSubprotocol(headers['sec-websocket-protocol']);
  if (!headers.authorization) return offered;
  const presented = authorizationToken(headers.authorization);
  // FR-037: HAL Engine hands tools the header, so a header naming anyone but the offered token's holder names no one.
  return offered === undefined || offered === presented ? presented : undefined;
}
</document>
<document source="apps/web/src/chat/halSocket.ts" type="code" relevance="0.98" tokens="129">
function connect(link: Link, socketUrl: string): WebSocket {
  const {webSocketCtor = globalThis.WebSocket} = link.options;
  // The token rides Sec-WebSocket-Protocol, the only header a browser lets a WebSocket carry, behind the marker the engine answers.
  const socket = new webSocketCtor(socketUrl, [HAL_WS_SUBPROTOCOL, link.token]);
  socket.onmessage = (event: MessageEvent<string>) => deliver(event.data, link.options);
  socket.onclose = (event: CloseEvent) => dropped(link, event.code);
  return socket;
}
</document>
<document source="apps/web/src/login/oidcLogin.ts" type="code" relevance="0.93" tokens="122">
// A login that rotates no refresh token keeps the one it was sent, as RFC 6749 §6 allows.
function tokensFrom(
  answer: Record<string, unknown> | null,
  now: number,
  heldRefreshToken: string | null
): LoginTokens | null {
  const accessToken = answer?.['access_token'];
  if (typeof accessToken !== 'string') return null;
  return {
    accessToken,
    refreshToken: stringOr(answer?.['refresh_token'], heldRefreshToken),
    expiresAt: expiryOf(answer?.['expires_in'], now),
  };
}
</document>
<document source="apps/api/src/oauth/httpAuth.ts" type="code" relevance="0.90" tokens="171">
// FR-029: the TMS tools verify the connection's bearer token, and no tool reads its cookie or host, so neither is held.
export function supportAgentAuth(verify: VerifyIdentity): HalEngineConfig['auth'] {
  return {
    // eslint-disable-next-line id-length -- HAL Engine names the WebSocket auth hook `ws`.
    ws: (request) => authenticateWebSocket(request, verify),
    http: denyChatRoutes,
    forwardHeaders: ['authorization'],
  };
}

export async function authenticateWebSocket(
  request: {headers: BearerHeaders},
  verify: VerifyIdentity
) {
  const identity = await verify(bearerTokenOf(request.headers));
  return identity === null ? null : authenticatedUser(identity);
}
</document>
<document source="apps/api/src/server.ts" type="code" relevance="0.50" tokens="19">
export {authenticateWebSocket, supportAgentAuth} from './oauth/httpAuth.js';
</document>
<document source="apps/web/src/login/useLogin.ts" type="code" relevance="0.46" tokens="65">
export interface Login {
  phase: LoginPhase;
  logIn: () => Promise<LoginStart>;
  logOut: () => void;
  // A token renewed now, for a socket reconnecting after a drop: one a restarted api signs with its new key.
  freshToken: () => Promise<string | null>;
}
</document>
</section>
<section name="Architecture Decisions" source="adrs" priority="2">
<document source="adrs/ADR-001-tms-authentication.md" type="adr" relevance="1.00" tokens="656">
## GDPR — data-flow update

This section updates the data-flow record (`support-conversation-data-flow-record`, Lore #6) with the credential as a data category.

**Credential category:** The OLT TMS API key (`TMS_API_KEY`) is a service credential (not personal data). It is read once at startup from the environment, held in process memory for the process lifetime, passed as `x-api-key` on every live TMS request, and never written to a log, audit row, tool result or error message (CR-003, enforced by `apps/api/src/shared/logger.ts` — the logger drops any field whose key names a payload, and a test asserts the redaction).

**Token (JWT) category:** The customer's access token is personal data (it names a user). It is held in `ChatSession.authHeaders` for the WebSocket connection's life only, never written to MongoDB, never logged, and leaves the process only through the resolver's `jwtVerify` call (a local verification, no network). It is not forwarded to the TMS.

**Retention:** The TMS API key has no expiry in our control; it lives until OLT rotates it. The customer's JWT is discarded when the WebSocket closes. No copy is written anywhere.

**Recipients:** The TMS API key is sent to OLT's TMS endpoint (`olt.dora-apps.com`) on every live request. No other recipient. The customer's JWT is verified locally and never forwarded.

**Login session category (stand-in only, added 2026-10-27, #614):** until RD-5 closes, the stand-in login keeps a session per browser so a reload or a restart signs nobody out. MongoDB's `loginSessions` holds the tester's name and SHA-256 hashes of the session cookie and of each refresh token, never the values and never a customer number, for at most 30 days, after which a TTL index removes it. The GDPR erasure command deletes a user's sessions. The real login will hold its own session on its own side.

No credential, token or `authorization` value is written to any log, browser storage or error message, with one exception: the stand-in login's own session cookie (#614). It is `HttpOnly`, so no script on the page can read it, and scoped to `/api/oauth`, so it never rides `/api/ws`, where HAL Engine reads request headers. A token in `localStorage` or `sessionStorage` would be readable by any script injected into the page, which is why the cookie is the least exposed way to survive a reload. The enforcement criteria are: `logger.ts` redaction (validated by test), `defineTmsTool.ts` returning a fixed string on resolver refusal (validated by `apps/api/test/defineTmsTool.test.ts`), and the audit trail writing metadata only, never content (`apps/api/src/audit/`).
</document>
</section>

- ADR-001 says the customer's JWT is never logged and is discarded when the socket closes. The api logger also redacts sensitive fields.

What is not protected:
- An ingress or proxy that captures request headers will record `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, just as it records an `Authorization` header. Header capture must redact `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` too.
- The token also exists in the upgrade request headers, the socket's and session's `authHeaders`, and the tool context. Anything that logs those, including a hook or tool, would leak it.
